name: blueprint-conventions
description: The LaTeX-subset blueprint format and house style — environments, \uses/\lean/\leanok/\mathlibok/\notready, the math-purity rule, and complete (not sketched) proofs.
---

Blueprints are a LaTeX subset (the `leanblueprint` dialect) parsed into the DAG.
Write timeless mathematics — a standalone document, not a project journal.

## Environments

Each declaration is an amsthm-style environment; the recognized ones are
`theorem`, `lemma`, `proposition`, `corollary`, `definition`, `remark`,
`example`, `notation`, `convention`, and `proof`. A statement environment plus
its following `proof` environment form one node's content.

## Per-node macros

- `\label{id}` — a stable id (the DAG node key).
- `\lean{Name}` — the Lean declaration(s) this node formalizes; comma-separate to
  bind several (`\lean{a, b}`) when they jointly formalize the node's statement.
  Each named declaration's signature must match the statement. The mapping need
  not be 1-to-1: a node may name several declarations, and Lean may carry
  auxiliary declarations with no node at all.
- `\uses{a,b}` — dependencies on other nodes' labels; these drive the DAG edges.
  Add an edge instead of re-explaining a dependency in prose. Put `\uses` in the
  statement for definitional deps and in the `proof` for deps used only in the
  proof.
- `\source{slug:page-0001}` — reference anchors for UI popups and audit trails.
  Use page-level ids from `references/<slug>/tex/page-0001.tex` or an equivalent
  manifest entry. Multiple anchors may be comma-separated.
- `\leanok` — the Lean is written and checked. Honest only when its Lean is
  actually checked *and* its dependencies are too. On a `proof`, it means the
  proof is formalized; on a statement, the signature is formalized.
- `\mathlibok` — the declaration is already available in mathlib (no
  formalization needed; treat as a leaf).
- `\notready` — the Lean is **not written yet**: the node's statement stands but
  no declaration formalizes it. Mutually exclusive with `\leanok` (a node is
  never both) — remove `\notready` exactly when you add `\leanok`, i.e. the
  moment its Lean is written and checked. It is a human-facing marker of an
  intentional gap, not a DAG edge.

## House style

- **Pure mathematics only.** No Lean tactics, typeclass/implementation notes, or
  semi-Lean pseudocode. No project history ("since iter N", "our failed route")
  and no conversational filler. Not every Lean helper needs its own node —
  auxiliary or implementation-only declarations can stay unnoded; add a node when
  the result is mathematically meaningful in its own right. In particular, never
  add a `Formalization note` paragraph to blueprint `.tex`: attach implementation
  details, failed approaches, and mechanization caveats to the statement's hgraph
  node with `horizon graph ... add comment` instead.
- **Complete proofs, not sketches.** A node's `proof` is a real, rigorous
  mathematical proof a reader could check — not a hand-wave or a TODO. The way to
  keep it short is to *split*, not to abbreviate: if a proof is long or a node
  grows past a short paragraph, break out the hard step as its own `\uses`-linked
  lemma (down to sentence-sized lemmas if needed) so each node stays small and
  its proof stays complete.
- **One statement's worth per node.** Keep each node to a single mathematical
  statement; don't restate Lean source as prose.
- **Cite by source link, not quote comments.** Add `\source{...}` to the
  relevant node. Keep the retrieved/transcribed page text in `references/` (for
  example `references/<slug>/tex/page-0042.tex`) and let the UI expose it; do not
  paste verbatim source quotes into `% QUOTE` comments inside the blueprint.

2	name: blueprint-conventions
3	description: The LaTeX-subset blueprint format and house style — environments, \uses/\lean/\leanok/\mathlibok/\notready, the math-purity rule, and complete (not sketched) proofs.
4	---
5	
6	Blueprints are a LaTeX subset (the `leanblueprint` dialect) parsed into the DAG.
7	Write timeless mathematics — a standalone document, not a project journal.
8	
9	## Environments
10	
11	Each declaration is an amsthm-style environment; the recognized ones are
12	`theorem`, `lemma`, `proposition`, `corollary`, `definition`, `remark`,
13	`example`, `notation`, `convention`, and `proof`. A statement environment plus
14	its following `proof` environment form one node's content.
15	
16	## Per-node macros
17	
18	- `\label{id}` — a stable id (the DAG node key).
19	- `\lean{Name}` — the Lean declaration(s) this node formalizes; comma-separate to
20	  bind several (`\lean{a, b}`) when they jointly formalize the node's statement.
21	  Each named declaration's signature must match the statement. The mapping need
22	  not be 1-to-1: a node may name several declarations, and Lean may carry
23	  auxiliary declarations with no node at all.
24	- `\uses{a,b}` — dependencies on other nodes' labels; these drive the DAG edges.
25	  Add an edge instead of re-explaining a dependency in prose. Put `\uses` in the
26	  statement for definitional deps and in the `proof` for deps used only in the
27	  proof.
28	- `\source{slug:page-0001}` — reference anchors for UI popups and audit trails.
29	  Use page-level ids from `references/<slug>/tex/page-0001.tex` or an equivalent
30	  manifest entry. Multiple anchors may be comma-separated.
31	- `\leanok` — the Lean is written and checked. Honest only when its Lean is
32	  actually checked *and* its dependencies are too. On a `proof`, it means the
33	  proof is formalized; on a statement, the signature is formalized.
34	- `\mathlibok` — the declaration is already available in mathlib (no
35	  formalization needed; treat as a leaf).
36	- `\notready` — the Lean is **not written yet**: the node's statement stands but
37	  no declaration formalizes it. Mutually exclusive with `\leanok` (a node is
38	  never both) — remove `\notready` exactly when you add `\leanok`, i.e. the
39	  moment its Lean is written and checked. It is a human-facing marker of an
40	  intentional gap, not a DAG edge.
41	
42	## House style
43	
44	- **Pure mathematics only.** No Lean tactics, typeclass/implementation notes, or
45	  semi-Lean pseudocode. No project history ("since iter N", "our failed route")
46	  and no conversational filler. Not every Lean helper needs its own node —
47	  auxiliary or implementation-only declarations can stay unnoded; add a node when
48	  the result is mathematically meaningful in its own right. In particular, never
49	  add a `Formalization note` paragraph to blueprint `.tex`: attach implementation
50	  details, failed approaches, and mechanization caveats to the statement's hgraph
51	  node with `horizon graph ... add comment` instead.
52	- **Complete proofs, not sketches.** A node's `proof` is a real, rigorous
53	  mathematical proof a reader could check — not a hand-wave or a TODO. The way to
54	  keep it short is to *split*, not to abbreviate: if a proof is long or a node
55	  grows past a short paragraph, break out the hard step as its own `\uses`-linked
56	  lemma (down to sentence-sized lemmas if needed) so each node stays small and
57	  its proof stays complete.
58	- **One statement's worth per node.** Keep each node to a single mathematical
59	  statement; don't restate Lean source as prose.
60	- **Cite by source link, not quote comments.** Add `\source{...}` to the
61	  relevant node. Keep the retrieved/transcribed page text in `references/` (for
62	  example `references/<slug>/tex/page-0042.tex`) and let the UI expose it; do not
63	  paste verbatim source quotes into `% QUOTE` comments inside the blueprint.

2	\label{chap:Genus}
3	
4	Throughout this chapter, \(k\) denotes a field and \(C\) a smooth proper geometrically irreducible curve over \(k\) of relative dimension \(1\). In other words, \(C \to \Spec k\) is a morphism of schemes carrying the geometric typeclasses that make it a curve in the modern sense.
5	
6	\section{Definition}
7	
8	% NOTE: classical definition \(g(C) = \dim_k H^1(C, \mathcal O_C)\); see
9	% Hartshorne, *Algebraic Geometry*, Ch.~IV \S1 (genus of a curve) — TOC
10	% summarised in `references/hartshorne-ag.md`. The finiteness backing
11	% (Serre on coherent cohomology of a proper \(k\)-scheme) is queued in
12	% `references/stacks-0BUG.md` and chapter

14	\begin{definition}[Genus of a smooth proper curve]\leanok
15	  \label{def:genus}
16	  \uses{def:Scheme_HModule, def:Scheme_toModuleKSheaf}
17	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.genus}
18	  
19	  The \emph{genus} of a smooth proper curve \(C\) over \(k\) is the natural number
20	  \[
21	    g(C) \;=\; \dim_k H^1(C,\, \mathcal O_C),
22	  \]
23	  the \(k\)-dimension of the first sheaf-cohomology group of the structure sheaf of \(C\).
24	\end{definition}
25	
26	\begin{proof}
27	  
28	  \leanok
29	  The definition is realised by passing the structure sheaf through the sheaf-of-\(k\)-modules construction and applying the \(k\)-linear sheaf cohomology \(H^1\). The result is a \(k\)-vector space; its dimension is extracted via the standard finiteness rank.
30	
31	  \begin{remark}[Lean implementation]
32	    The formal definition uses the project's \(\ModuleCat k\)-flavoured sheaf cohomology of the structure sheaf:
33	    \[
34	      \mathtt{genus}\,C \;:=\; \Module.\mathtt{finrank}\,k\,\bigl(\Scheme.\HModule\,k\,(\Scheme.\toModuleKSheaf\,C)\,1\bigr).
35	    \]
36	    The carrier \(\toModuleKSheaf C\) is the sheaf-of-\(k\)-modules constructed from \(\struct C\) via the structure morphism; the wrapper \(\HModule k F 1\) is the \(\Module k\)-flavoured sheaf cohomology, given by \(\Ext\) from the constant sheaf at \(\ModuleCat.\mathrm{of}\,k\,k\), which carries a canonical \(\Module k\)-structure inherited from the \(\Linear k\)-enrichment of the sheaf category.
37	  \end{remark}
38	
39	  Mathlib's \(\Module.\mathtt{finrank}\) returns the \(k\)-dimension when the underlying module is finite-dimensional and zero otherwise. For a smooth proper geometrically irreducible curve, Serre's theorem on coherent cohomology of a proper \(k\)-scheme guarantees \(\dim_k H^1(C, \struct C) < \infty\), so \(g(C)\) is the geometric genus on the relevant case. The closure is therefore the one-liner above, confirmed to typecheck against current Mathlib.
40	\end{proof}
41	
42	Equivalent reformulations available once Riemann--Roch and Serre duality are formalised:
43	\begin{itemize}
44	  \item \(g(C) = \dim_k H^0(C,\, \Omega^1_{C/k})\) (Serre duality).
45	  \item \(g(C) = 1 - \chi(\mathcal O_C)\), where \(\chi\) is the Euler characteristic.
46	  \item For a smooth projective curve over \(\mathbb C\), \(g(C)\) equals the topological genus of \(C(\mathbb C)\).
47	\end{itemize}
48	Each of these requires Mathlib infrastructure that is currently absent. The first reformulation in particular requires the sheaf of relative differentials of schemes (Phase~B), and the others require Riemann--Roch / Serre duality / a topological-vs-algebraic geometry comparison.

/-! ## Project-local Mathlib supplement — Quot/Grassmannian predicates

These declarations build the support/freeness predicates of
`blueprint/src/chapters/Picard_QuotScheme.tex`, §"Support and freeness
predicates". Mathlib (at the pinned commit) carries no rank-`d` local
freeness predicate for sheaves of modules on a scheme, so it is built here. -/

namespace SheafOfModules

/-- **Locally free of rank `d`** for a sheaf of modules on a scheme.

A sheaf of modules `M` on a scheme `X` is *locally free of rank `d`* when `X`
admits an open cover `{U i}` on each member of which the restriction
`M|_{U i}` (the pullback of `M` along the open immersion `(U i).ι`) is
isomorphic to the free module of rank `d`, `O_{U i}^{⊕ d}` (encoded as
`SheafOfModules.free (ULift (Fin d))` over the structure-ring sheaf of the
open subscheme `(U i).toScheme`).

This predicate is project-local: Mathlib does not supply a rank-indexed local
freeness predicate for sheaves of modules on a scheme. Blueprint:
`def:is_locally_free_of_rank` (Nitsure §1, Exercise (2)). -/
def IsLocallyFreeOfRank {X : Scheme.{u}} (M : X.Modules) (d : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ (ι : Type u) (U : ι → X.Opens), (⨆ i, U i = ⊤) ∧
    ∀ i, Nonempty ((Scheme.Modules.pullback (U i).ι).obj M ≅
      _root_.SheafOfModules.free (R := (U i).toScheme.ringCatSheaf) (ULift.{u} (Fin d)))

end SheafOfModules

     9	\section{Auxiliary existence predicates}
    10	\label{sec:fga_pic_typeclass_scaffolding}
    11	
    12	The public constructions use a small collection of existence predicates. Each
    13	predicate records one mathematical object or property needed by the preceding
    14	representability argument, and the associated definitions select the object
    15	when the predicate is inhabited.
    16	
    17	\subsection{Basic functors}
    18	\label{subsec:fga_pic_functor_carriers}
    19	
    20	\begin{definition}[\(k\)-rational point]\leanok
    21	  \label{def:has_rational_point}
    22	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme.HasRationalPoint}
    23	  The predicate \(\mathrm{HasRationalPoint}(C)\) asserts that the structural
    24	  morphism \(C \to \Spec k\) admits a section
    25	  \(\sigma : \Spec k \to C\), i.e.\ that \(C\) has a \(k\)-rational point.
    26	  This is the standing hypothesis of the chapter (see
    27	  \cref{sec:fga_pic_setup}): by Kleiman \S 2, Thm.~2.5, it makes the plain
    28	  relative Picard functor \(\Pic^\sharp_{C/k}\) coincide with its \'etale
    29	  (and fppf) sheafification, so representability can be stated against
    30	  \cref{def:rel_pic_sharp} directly. For a pointed curve \((C,P)\), the
    31	  pointing \(P\) supplies this section.
    32	\end{definition}

    49	\section{Dependencies of the representability theorem}
    50	\label{sec:fga_pic_sorry_closure_order}
    51	
    52	The construction of \(\Pic_{C/k}\) separates into three mathematical inputs:
    53	the relative-divisor functor, its Abel map to the relative Picard functor, and
    54	the FGA existence theorem. The first two supply concrete functors and a
    55	natural transformation. The third combines them with regularity, cohomology
    56	and base change, and effective descent to produce a scheme locally of finite
    57	type representing \(\Pic^\sharp_{C/k}\).
    58	
    59	\subsection{The Picard-scheme existence theorem}
    60	\label{subsec:sorry_has_pic_scheme}
    61	
    62	For a
    63	smooth proper geometrically integral curve \(C/k\) with a \(k\)-rational
    64	point, the relative Picard functor \(\Pic^\sharp_{C/k}\)
    65	(\cref{def:pic_sharp_carrier}) is representable by a \(k\)-scheme. Either route
    66	of \cref{sec:fga_pic_setup} establishes it, and they consume different inputs.
    67	
    68	Along the Milne--Koll\'ar route of \cref{sec:fga_pic_milne_kollar} --- the one
    69	being formalised --- the inputs are: the rigidified pushforward
    70	\cref{thm:rigid_pushforward_gate}, which holds for every curve satisfying this
    71	chapter's hypotheses and supplies both the canonical divisor family and the
    72	semicontinuity of \(h^0\) cutting out the loci \(C^\Sigma\); uniform \(H^1\) vanishing in high degree, which makes those loci
    73	cover; representability of the degree-\(r\) divisor functor, which supplies the
    74	ambient \(Z\) together with its Grassmannian immersion; and the finite Galois
    75	quotient \cref{thm:galois_quotient_points} with
    76	\cref{lem:stable_affine_open}, which descends the result from a separably closed
    77	field to \(k\). No Hilbert or Quot scheme occurs among them.
    78	
    79	Along the quotient route the proof first applies Kleiman \S 2, Thm.~2.5, using
    80	the section to identify the plain functor with its \'etale sheafification, and
    81	then uses Kleiman's four steps
    82	(\cref{thm:fga_pic_representability}): Hilbert-polynomial stratification,
    83	\(m\)-regularity bound, Abel-map factorisation through
    84	\(\mathrm{Div}_{C/k}\), and the smooth-proper quotient
    85	(\cref{lem:smooth_proper_quotient}). Its inputs are the Quot/Hilbert
    86	construction of \cref{chap:Picard_QuotScheme}, representability of
    87	\(\mathrm{Div}_{C/k}\) as in \cref{rem:div_functor_representability}, the
    88	regularity result \cref{cor:flattening_stratification_curve}, the base-change
    89	result \cref{lem:cech_flat_base_change}, and Altman--Kleiman effective descent.
    90	Both routes rest on the same divisor and comparison substrate, and the
    91	rational-point hypothesis enters both in the same way.
    92	
    93	Either way, the resulting representing object gives
    94	natural bijections
    95	\[
    96	  (T\to\Pic_{C/k})\simeq
    97	  \Pic(C\times_kT)/\pi_T^*\Pic(T),
    98	\]
    99	including the dual-number case \(T=\Spec k[\epsilon]\) used in the
   100	tangent-space calculation.
   101	
   102	\subsection{The relative-divisor input}
   103	\label{subsec:sorry_has_div_functor}
   104	
   105	The relative-divisor functor \(\Div_{X/S}\) of
   106	\cref{def:div_functor} is the subfunctor of the Hilbert functor
   107	\(\Hilb_{C/k} = \Quot_{\mathcal{O}_C/C/k}\) of relative effective Cartier
   108	divisors, in the invertible-kernel quotient encoding of
   109	\cref{def:div_family}. The presheaf \(\mathrm{Div}_{C/k}\) of
   110	\cref{def:div_functor_carrier} is its instantiation at
   111	\(C\to\Spec k\). Its divisor condition is stable under base change by
   112	\cref{lem:relative_divisor_base_change}, while representability of
   113	\(\Div_{C/k}\) by an open subscheme of the Hilbert scheme (Kleiman \S 3,
   114	Thm.~th:repDiv) is the content of
   115	\cref{rem:div_functor_representability}.
   116	
   117	\subsection{The Abel-map input}
   118	\label{subsec:sorry_has_abel_map}
   119	
   120	The class \cref{def:has_abel_map} carries the natural transformation whose
   121	value on a divisor family is
   122	\[
   123	  \mathrm{abelMapWitness}(C)\langle\mathcal F,q\rangle=-[\ker q].
   124	\]
   125	It is the composite of the kernel-class natural transformation
   126	\(\mathrm{abelKernelNatTrans}(C)\) (naturality via the kernel--flat-base-change
   127	comparison isomorphism) with the group-presheaf negation
   128	\(\mathrm{picNeg}(C)\). Thus the Abel map has the defining property in
   129	\cref{lem:line_bundle_quot_correspondence}; it is a natural transformation
   130	of the presheaves in \cref{def:div_functor_carrier} and
   131	\cref{def:pic_sharp_carrier}.
   132	
   133	\subsection{Assembly of the inputs}
   134	\label{subsec:fga_pic_closure_order_summary}
   135	
   136	The FGA construction consumes the relative-divisor functor and Abel map,
   137	then applies the regularity, base-change, and effective-quotient results of
   138	\cref{thm:fga_pic_representability}. A pointing
   139	\(P:\mathbf 1\to C\) supplies the rational-point hypothesis used to identify
   140	the plain relative Picard functor with its sheafification. The resulting
   141	representability and local-finiteness statements feed the group-scheme and
   142	Jacobian constructions.
   143	
   144	\section{Related constructions}
   145	\label{sec:fga_pic_out_of_scope}
   146	
   147	The representable Picard scheme and its group structure interact with the
   148	following constructions, treated in the indicated companion chapters.
   149	\begin{itemize}
   150	  \item \textbf{Identity component \(\Pic^0_{C/k}\)} --- the open and
   151	    closed subgroup scheme of \(\Pic_{C/k}\) containing the unit and
   152	    consisting of those classes lying in the connected component of
   153	    \(\Pic_{C/k}\). Its dimension, smoothness, and abelian-variety
   154	    structure are treated in \cref{chap:Picard_IdentityComponent} and
   155	    \cref{chap:Picard_Pic0AbelianVariety}.
